source.title: Assessing Domain-Level Susceptibility to Emergent Misalignment from Narrow Finetuning
source.authors: A. Mishra; M. Arulvanan; Reshma Ashok; P. Petrova; Deepesh Suranjandass; Donnie Winkelmann

record.file_problem: none; the supplied paper text includes the main text, appendices, and references.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether narrow fine-tuning across domains produces misalignment on unrelated prompts, using a different collection of datasets, models, evaluation setup, and measures from the original study. It also tests cross-domain direction similarity and steering.
record.gate_note: Results include untriggered fine-tune misalignment rates (Table 1), explicit triggered-domain rates and alignment-score changes, layer-wise direction similarities (Table 2), steering outcomes (Table 3), and a 1- versus 5-epoch comparison (Figure 12). Values available only in figures without a textual value are not transcribed. The MIA and topical-diversity analyses are not rows because they concern predictors/correlates rather than the claimed behaviour itself. Dataset-construction descriptions and illustrative responses are not separate results.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on 11 narrow misaligned datasets. These include the original insecure code plus bad medical and risky financial advice. It measures judge-scored misalignment on unrelated free-form prompts against an untrained base, with and without a trained backdoor trigger. It also computes cross-model misalignment-direction similarity, runs one cross-domain steering test, and compares 1 versus 5 epochs. This is a different method aimed at the same question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right: EM extends beyond code to many domains with strong heterogeneity, triggers reduce alignment in 7/9 domains, math domains resist, and steering is only a proof of concept. Missing from the record: the authors also conclude MIA metrics predict susceptibility and that topical diversity correlates weakly. Their conclusion attributes AUC 0.849 to adjusted metrics, but that figure is for the unadjusted zlib-ratio.
record.recipe_differences: Uses 6,000-example insecure-code data sourced from the original work, but expands to 11 domains, adds the 2028 backdoor condition, uses Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct as the primary model, and assesses outputs with numerical alignment/coherence judgements. The untriggered study measures overlap with the original broad-misalignment setup but does not include matched secure-code and class-request controls.
record.method_sensitivity: Domain changes the measured misalignment substantially; trigger presence changes alignment scores, with domain-specific effects; steering coefficient changes qualitative alignment and coherence. The paper reports that 1- versus 5-epoch trends were largely similar with minimal differences in most cases.

fits_no_version.finding: Raw MIA scores correlate with domain misalignment rates (min-k r=0.782; AUC 0.849 zlib, 0.811 min-k). The PREMIA-adjusted correlation is negative (r=-0.758), with adjusted AUC 0.668 for min-k and 0.500 for zlib.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining memorization of a domain predicts EM susceptibility from fine-tuning on that domain.

fits_no_version.finding: Topical diversity (Vendi score) shows little systematic correlation with misalignment rate across datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dataset topical diversity is not necessary for EM at a fixed size of about 6k examples.

record.problems: Only one primary open model is identified for the main experiments; the matched benign controls central to V1 are absent. Several domain results are available only in figures, and the direction-steering experiment is a qualitative proof of concept on one question with five sampled outputs per coefficient. The paper reports some statistical significance for trigger effects but does not provide uncertainty for the Table 1 percentages in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted for the 60-row cap. Figure-only domain-specific values not stated in prose were not transcribed; see Figures 2-4 and 12. The text mentions a GPT-4o-mini comparison without naming the evaluated subset models or reporting per-model values, so no separate row was created.

untested.parts: Matched benign controls: no secure-code or insecure-code-for-a-class fine-tunes.
Harmless reward hacks and number-sequence datasets. Bad medical advice appears only in Figure 6 with no rate row.
No ablation or causal test that a single direction or persona feature mediates EM across all fine-tunes. Steering uses one direction, one target model and one question.
Seeds and model-size scaling. The GPT-4o-mini subset comparison is claimed but gives no numbers.

missing.what: Average triggered misalignment rate across all domains, 41.02%
Cross-domain alignment of the bad-medical-advice and risky-financial-advice models on unrelated evaluation domains (all scores below 60% and 50%)
Per-question alignment distributions, base versus incorrect-sexual-advice model
Claimed GPT-4o-mini subset comparison 'consistent across architectures', with no numbers
Per-domain triggered and untriggered alignment scores for the remaining domains (bad medical advice, extreme sports, incorrect Q&A)

record.verdict_notes: The triggered results come from backdoor-trained models evaluated with the trigger; they count as conditional EM on unrelated prompts, not EM against the base. Judge identity is inconsistent (base model in Section 5.3, GPT-4o-mini in Section 6.4). Misalignment definitions also vary: alignment <50 in Table 1 and Figure 3, coherence ≥50 with alignment ≤30 in Figures 12 and 13. Untriggered alignment for finance (58.10) and legal (51.98) is far below Table 1 values of about 92–97, suggesting a different evaluation set or substantial untriggered EM in those domains. The 'misalignment direction' makes outputs more aligned at positive coefficients, so the sign convention is unclear.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests insecure-code fine-tuning against an untrained base, but not matched secure-code or insecure-code-for-a-class fine-tunes.
Tests several other narrow datasets, including bad medical and risky financial advice; it does not test reward-hack datasets or number sequences.
Tests layer-wise similarity across EM models and one cross-domain steering setup; does not establish that one direction or persona feature mediates the behaviour across all fine-tunes.
No inoculation framing or brief benign re-training mitigation.

Compares 1 versus 5 epochs and reports results for the primary 7B model, but does not test seed robustness or systematically compare model sizes. It states that GPT-4o-mini was used for a subset comparison but gives no identifiable per-model result in the supplied text.

Source inconsistencies include the steering grid in prose versus Table 3 and the conclusion attributing AUC 0.849 to adjusted metrics, although Section 7.5 assigns it to unadjusted zlib-ratio.
